function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
I’ve written the three files that you asked for (Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, GitHub‑Actions workflow) and then given you a short step‑by‑step guide on how to add them to the repo, commit, and push.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git add`, `git commit` or `git push` for you, but the commands below will get you there.

---

## 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Analyse the repo

The repo contains a very small Node.js app (`app.js`) and a `package.json`.  
It listens on port **3000** (see `app.js`).

---

## 3. Create the required files

### 3.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image as the base
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why Node 18?*  
> The latest LTS release at the time of writing is Node 18. Feel free to bump the tag if you prefer a different version.

---

### 3.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` (or any name you like) in the root of the repo with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *What this does:*  
> * Deployment: 2 replicas of the container, each listening on port 3000.  
> * Service: Exposes the pods on port 80 inside the cluster (you can change `type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access).

---

### 3.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'   # match Dockerfile base image

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

  docker-build-push:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest .
          docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password) with push rights to the `zelarhq` namespace.

---

## 4. Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 5. Commit and push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the next commit to `main`, building the Docker image, running tests, and pushing the image to Docker Hub.

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Actions** tab with a successful run.  
* In Docker Hub, the image `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` (and a SHA‑tagged image) should appear.  
* You can deploy the Kubernetes manifest with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
```

---

That’s it! Let me know if you’d like help tweaking any of the files or adding more advanced CI steps.
